analysis.one_liner: Caps punitive damages and rewrites product liability rules nationwide to shield product makers and sellers from lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill passed both chambers—265-161 in the House and 61-37 in the Senate—and cleared a conference committee, but President Clinton vetoed it and the House fell short of the two-thirds majority needed to override, 258-163.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced state product-liability rules with a uniform national system that makes it harder and less rewarding to sue a product maker or seller. It would cap punitive damages (generally at twice compensatory damages or $250,000, whichever is larger), make each defendant pay only its own percentage share of pain-and-suffering damages, bar most lawsuits filed more than two years after the injury is discovered or 20 years after the product was sold, and give sellers near-total immunity unless they were careless, broke their own warranty, or acted intentionally. It would also shield the companies that supply raw materials for medical implants from most lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, product sellers, medical-implant material suppliers, and liability insurers gain the most: caps and time limits on damages, reduced exposure for distributors and suppliers, and predictable nationwide rules lower the cost of losing or settling a lawsuit.

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages at the greater of twice compensatory damages or $250,000, with a lower effective cap for small defendants, unless a judge finds in a separate proceeding that the cap would not punish or deter egregious conduct.
Makes each defendant pay only its proportionate share of noneconomic damages (pain and suffering), instead of the full amount when other responsible parties cannot pay.
Gives product sellers near-immunity: they are liable only for negligence, breach of an express warranty, or intentional wrongdoing, and a lack of opportunity to inspect is not negligence.
Sets uniform deadlines: most suits must be filed within two years of discovering the harm, and no suit over a durable good can be filed more than 20 years after delivery.

Bars suits against biomaterials suppliers for harm caused by implants unless the supplier failed to meet contractual specifications, manufactured or sold the implant itself, or fraudulently concealed information—responding to congressional findings that suppliers had stopped selling materials for implants because of litigation costs.

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products: lower maximum recoveries, less ability to collect full damages when one defendant is broke or judgment-proof, shorter windows to sue, and new defenses—including a complete defense if the injured person was intoxicated and more than 50 percent at fault.

drawbacks.text: The two-year limit and 20-year cutoff would bar legitimate claims—especially for injuries that appear long after exposure, such as toxic harm from products bought decades earlier.

Several-only liability means an injured person cannot collect the full pain-and-suffering award from the one defendant who can actually pay when other responsible parties are bankrupt or judgment-proof.

Sellers and suppliers escape liability even when the injured person has no practical recourse against the original manufacturer—though the bill does make a seller liable as a manufacturer if the maker cannot be served or a judgment against it could not be enforced.

The punitive cap, applied by the judge and hidden from the jury, limits the main tool for deterring and punishing conduct a jury finds reckless; supporters counter that without limits, unpredictable verdicts raise prices, chill innovation, and—as Congress found for implant materials—drive suppliers out of markets for lifesaving devices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real gains for producers—predictable rules, caps, and reduced exposure for peripheral sellers and suppliers—and its biomaterials provisions respond to a genuine documented problem of materials disappearing from the medical device market. But the cost falls on people who are most badly hurt: those with the largest injuries and those suing long-lived or toxic products lose the most. The bill shifts risk from companies to injured consumers, with no offsetting compensation, price control, or safety mechanism to protect the people who give up their claims.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 265-161, the Senate 61-37, and both chambers approved the final conference report—but President Clinton vetoed it, and the House's override vote of 258-163 fell short of the two-thirds needed to enact the bill over his objection.

narrative.text: Introduced in February 1995, the bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee 31-11 within a week and reached the House floor in March.
The House passed it on March 10, 1995, 265-161, with Republicans voting 220-6 for it and Democrats 45-154 against.

A Democrats' motion to recommit—raising the punitive cap to $1 million and requiring foreign manufacturers to appoint a U.S. agent for lawsuits—failed 195-231, with 189 of 204 Democrats in favor and only 5 Republicans.
The Senate rewrote the bill, added an alternative-dispute-resolution offer process and a Biomaterials Access Assurance title, and passed it 61-37 on May 10, 1995.

House Democrats twice tried to steer the conference—to protect higher recoveries for women, children, and the elderly (190-231) and to keep House language extending U.S. jurisdiction over foreign manufacturers (adopted 256-142)—before the conference report passed the Senate 59-40 on March 21, 1996, and the House 259-158 on March 29, 1996.
President Clinton vetoed the bill on May 2, 1996; the House override vote of 258-163 on May 9 fell well short of the two-thirds required, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products keep the full protections of their state laws, since no federal caps or time limits ever took effect. Product manufacturers, sellers, and insurers lost the liability limits they had pushed through both chambers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers; manufacturers lost the caps

for.name: Rep. Henry Hyde
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, steered it through committee markup in under a week, moved to reject the Senate version and request a conference, and managed the veto override attempt.

for.name: 220 of 229 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for passage on the House floor.

for.name: 46 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for Senate passage and for the conference report; Senate Republicans carried the floor debate, offering most of the amendments.

for.name: Product manufacturers and business groups
for.what_they_did: Ran a years-long campaign for federal limits on product-liability lawsuits, the top legislative priority for many manufacturing trade groups that session.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on May 2, 1996, after both chambers passed it.

against.name: 154 of 204 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, and 157 of 197 voted against overriding the veto.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Moved to instruct House conferees to reject any provision limiting recoveries for women, children, and the elderly, and repeatedly pressed to keep House language subjecting foreign manufacturers to U.S. lawsuits.

against.name: Rep. Bart Gordon
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to raise the punitive damages cap from $250,000 to $1 million and require foreign manufacturers to appoint a U.S. agent for service of process; the motion failed 195-231.

against.name: 31 of 46 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against Senate passage, and offered amendments to soften the bill, most of which were tabled.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous in favor—220-6 in the House and 46-7 in the Senate—while most Democrats opposed it (45-154 in the House, 15-30 in the Senate); the bill passed because Republicans held majorities in both chambers, and it died when 157 of 197 House Democrats voted against overriding the veto.

industries.note: The bill caps what they can be made to pay, sets hard deadlines on claims, and largely immunizes non-manufacturer sellers. The cost of that protection is borne by people injured by defective products, who would recover less or be shut out entirely.

The bill shields suppliers of raw materials for implants from almost all lawsuits, with narrow exceptions for violating contract specifications or fraud. Congress justified it by finding that litigation risk had driven suppliers out of the implant market and threatened the supply of lifesaving devices—but the shield also removes a remedy for patients harmed by implant materials.

Damage caps, proportionate-share rules, and shorter claim windows shrink payouts on product-injury claims. The bill also grants workers' compensation insurers a subrogation right to recover benefits from manufacturers, though it bars employers from using that to blame injured workers without a court finding of clear-and-convincing fault.
Fewer viable suits, shorter deadlines, and capped awards cut directly into the business of representing injured consumers, the group the bill's opponents argued it was designed to protect.
